channel.title: The Word from Nine Point Labs
channel.description: Release notes and build logs from Nine Point Labs: small, useful software for Linux, and for people who like to write.

item.title: Seven Nine Point Labs apps now run on any Linux, with AppImages
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Nine Point Labs apps are made for Omarchy first, and that isn’t changing. But they shouldn’t stop at Omarchy. As of today, seven of them also run on Ubuntu, Fedora, openSUSE and most other Linux distributions: every release now comes with an AppImage that runs on most x86_64 Linux systems and fits properly into your desktop.
item.content:encoded:
Nine Point Labs apps are made for Omarchy first, and that isn’t changing. But they shouldn’t stop at Omarchy. As of today, seven of them also run on Ubuntu, Fedora, openSUSE and most other Linux distributions: every release now comes with an AppImage that runs on most x86_64 Linux systems and fits properly into your desktop.

What’s new

These releases went out today, each with a -x86_64.AppImage attached next to the usual packages:

  • Repokase 0.2.5
  • Jubako 0.4.7
  • Dogear 0.1.1
  • omaforge 0.2.6
  • Rune 0.8.6
  • Bahá’í Reader 0.1.4
  • Hyprfall 0.1.4

The Python and Qt apps carry their own Python and Qt inside the AppImage, and Hyprfall carries its own Quickshell and Qt, so there’s nothing else to install. They run on most systems from about 2021 or 2022 on (glibc 2.34 or newer, 2.35 for Hyprfall): Ubuntu 22.04 and later, Debian 12 and later, Fedora, openSUSE and others.

It behaves like a real app

Download it, make it executable and run it:

chmod +x dogear-0.1.1-x86_64.AppImage
./dogear-0.1.1-x86_64.AppImage --install-desktop-entry

--install-desktop-entry puts the app in your application menu with its proper icon, so it shows up correctly in your launcher, taskbar and dock. Dogear also offers itself for PDFs, and Jubako opens .jubadb files. If you’d rather let a tool manage it, Gear Lever and AppImageLauncher both pick these up. Each AppImage has a .sha256 and a .zsync file next to it for checking and updating.

A few app-specific notes

  • Repokase and Dogear now follow your desktop’s light or dark setting when they’re not on Omarchy. On Omarchy they still follow your theme.
  • Dogear 0.1.1 also adds an About screen and works better in narrow windows, like half a screen in a tiling window manager.
  • Rune 0.8.6 packages for Arch, Debian and Fedora now install Rune’s AppStream info and icons in every size, so software centers and menus show it properly.
  • Bahá’í Reader 0.1.4 adds a Flatpak bundle as well, bahai-reader-0.1.4-x86_64.flatpak. It brings its own Python and GTK through the GNOME runtime, so it runs even where your system GTK is too old. It’s a download on the release page, not a Flathub listing. If your system’s Python or GTK is too old for the AppImage, the AppImage now tells you so and points you to the Flatpak.
  • Hyprfall 0.1.4 now needs Quickshell 0.3 or newer. Fedora’s Quickshell is older than that, so the Fedora package is gone and Fedora players should use the AppImage, which brings Quickshell 0.3.2 with it.

Get them

On Omarchy and Arch, nothing changes: install the .pkg.tar.zst from the release, or let Autonomix CLI pick the right download and keep the app updated:

autonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/dogear

On any other Linux, grab the AppImage from the release pages above. From here on, every new Nine Point Labs desktop app release ships an AppImage, and a Flatpak bundle will join it on the release page starting with each app’s next release.

item.title: Autonomix CLI 0.4.3: one password prompt for Update All
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: If you track several GitHub-release apps with Autonomix CLI and hit “Update All”, you probably met the same password dialog over and over. 0.4.3 fixes that: updating several apps now asks for your admin password once.
item.content:encoded:
If you track several GitHub-release apps with Autonomix CLI and hit “Update All”, you probably met the same password dialog over and over. 0.4.3 fixes that: updating several apps now asks for your admin password once.

What changed

Before, autonomix-cli update (and “Update All” from the Omarchy bar widget) installed each update on its own, so polkit asked for your password once per app. Now it downloads every update first, then installs them all in a single pacman -U, apt-get install or rpm -Uvh call. One install, one prompt.

Failures are clearer too:

  • A failed download only affects that app. It’s reported as failed, and the rest still install.
  • A failed install names everything in it. If the combined install fails, every app in the batch is reported with the installer’s error.
  • Cancelling says so. Closing the polkit dialog now shows “authentication cancelled” instead of a bare exit code.

The --json output is unchanged, so the bar widget keeps working as it is. No update needed on that side.

Also new since the last post

0.4.2 added an About screen. Press i in the TUI to see the version, the MIT license, a support email and a privacy statement, or run autonomix-cli about from the command line.

Get it

Autonomix CLI tracks itself, so if you already have it:

autonomix-cli update

New here? Add it once and it keeps itself current:

autonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/autonomix-cli

Packages for Arch, Debian/Ubuntu and Fedora (amd64 and arm64) are on the v0.4.3 release.

item.title: Dogear: a PDF reader for studying, made for Omarchy
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Class handouts, workbooks and textbooks mostly arrive as PDFs now, and most PDF readers treat them as something to look at, not something to work in. Dogear does what you’d do to a paper textbook: highlight in several colors, write notes next to what you highlighted, fold the corner of a page, and fill in the blanks on a worksheet. When you’re done, it exports everything to Markdown, for example straight into your Obsidian vault.
item.content:encoded:
Class handouts, workbooks and textbooks mostly arrive as PDFs now, and most PDF readers treat them as something to look at, not something to work in. Dogear does what you’d do to a paper textbook: highlight in several colors, write notes next to what you highlighted, fold the corner of a page, and fill in the blanks on a worksheet. When you’re done, it exports everything to Markdown, for example straight into your Obsidian vault.

dogear.ninepointlabs.com (with a narrated demo video) · v0.1.0 on GitHub

Mark it up like paper

Select text and press 1 through 5 to highlight it in yellow, green, blue, pink or purple, or press a to highlight and write a note in one go. Hover a highlight to read its note; notes also show in the sidebar and as markers in the margin. Press b to bookmark a page (it gets a folded corner, named after its table of contents entry), and keep general notes about the whole document with Ctrl+N.

Dogear remembers the page, scroll position and zoom for every file, so opening a handout again puts you back where you stopped.

Fill in the blanks

This is what sets Dogear apart. Worksheets leave lines for answers, and in Dogear you just click the line and type. There’s no text box to place: it finds the line in the rendered page (drawn rules, runs of underscores, dotted lines), writes on it in blue ink at the size of the page’s own text, and shrinks a long answer to fit a short blank. Tab jumps to the next blank, so a whole fill-in-the-blank page can be done from the keyboard. Ruled lines under a question become one answer that wraps from line to line.

A library that remembers your marks

With no PDF open, Dogear shows a library of every PDF you’ve opened, with how many highlights, notes, answers and bookmarks each has. Search reaches inside your marks too, so a word you highlighted three weeks ago finds its handout. You can sort, file documents under categories, and give them your own names (“Book 3: Children’s Classes” instead of a 60-character file name) without renaming the file.

Dogear never changes your PDFs. It keeps a copy of every PDF you mark up, so your marks always have their PDF even if the original is moved or deleted. Everything lives in one folder, ~/Documents/Dogear by default, that you can sync between computers with Syncthing, Dropbox or Google Drive. If two computers change the same document before syncing, Dogear merges the conflict copy back in and keeps every mark from both. It also notices a re-download or new edition of a book you’ve marked up and offers to bring your marks over.

Into Obsidian

Ctrl+E writes a Markdown file per PDF: document notes first, then one section per page with highlights as quotes (page and color included), each note under its highlight, bookmarks, and every worksheet answer under its full question, so the export reads without the PDF. Categories come along as Obsidian tags. Point the export folder at your vault in Settings and your study notes land where the rest of your notes live.

Native to Omarchy

Dogear is keyboard first, with Vim-style reading keys (j/k, J/K for pages, / to search) and Ctrl for commands, leaving Super to Hyprland. It follows your Omarchy theme and repaints the moment you run omarchy theme set, and it makes room in narrow tiling windows. No account, no network access and no telemetry.

Install v0.1.0

On Arch and Omarchy, install it with autonomix-cli, which also keeps it updated from GitHub Releases:

autonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/dogear

Or download dogear-0.1.0-1-any.pkg.tar.zst from the release page and run sudo pacman -U dogear-0.1.0-1-any.pkg.tar.zst. pacman pulls in pyside6 and qt6-webengine (for the Qt PDF library). Dogear then shows up in your app launcher and can open PDFs from the file manager.

MIT licensed. Questions or bugs go to help@ninepointlabs.com or the issue tracker.

item.title: folderblog 0.2.3: Better link previews, optional visitor counts, and safer deploys
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: folderblog turns a folder of Markdown into a live blog the moment you save. Two releases since the last word here, 0.2.2 and 0.2.3, make what it publishes look better when it’s shared and searched, add an opt-in visitor counter, and stop a blog kept in git from deploying half-finished work.
item.content:encoded:
folderblog turns a folder of Markdown into a live blog the moment you save. Two releases since the last word here, 0.2.2 and 0.2.3, make what it publishes look better when it’s shared and searched, add an opt-in visitor counter, and stop a blog kept in git from deploying half-finished work.

Share images for every post

Add image: to a post’s front matter, either a path inside the blog or a full URL, and it becomes that post’s og:image and twitter:image. folderblog writes it as an absolute URL and adds the width and height when the file lives in the blog. Posts without one fall back to static/og-default.png, or to a new optional image key in blog.toml.

---
title: "My post"
image: img/cover.jpg
---

folderblog check warns when the image doesn’t exist, so a typo doesn’t quietly ship a broken preview card.

Search engines get the whole picture

The default theme now gives every page a meta description, a canonical link, the full set of OpenGraph tags, and a twitter:card. Post pages carry BlogPosting structured data (JSON-LD), and the home page has a single h1 with the site title.

folderblog also writes a robots.txt by default that allows everything and points to the sitemap. If your blog has its own static/robots.txt, or your theme provides one, yours wins. And check now warns when blog.toml has no description.

If you keep your own copy of the theme in theme/, your templates are left alone. Copy the new default theme’s _layouts/base.html and post.html to pick up the tags, and run folderblog agents-md --write in each blog folder to refresh its AGENTS.md.

Optional visitor counts with GoatCounter

Want to know whether anyone reads the thing? Add one section to blog.toml:

[analytics]
goatcounter = "https://you.goatcounter.com"

Every rendered page gets GoatCounter’s cookie-free counting script, with any theme and no template edits. It’s off by default: with no [analytics] section the output is byte-for-byte what it was before. It’s never added by preview or build --drafts, so your own drafting doesn’t count as visits, and check flags an invalid URL.

Hold deploys while you’re mid-git

0.2.2 added deploy_branch for blog folders you keep in git:

deploy_branch = "main"

With it set, folderblog only deploys while the folder is a checkout of that branch. On another branch, a detached HEAD, or in the middle of a merge, rebase or cherry-pick, the deploy is held and shows as held: ... in folderblog status. It retries on its own once you’re back on the branch. Leave it unset and nothing changes. This blog runs with it on.

One note for both releases: older versions reject unknown keys in blog.toml, so upgrade before adding image, [analytics] or deploy_branch.

Grab it

SystemCommand
Arch / Omarchysudo pacman -U folderblog-bin-0.2.3-1-x86_64.pkg.tar.zst
Debian / Ubuntusudo apt install ./folderblog_0.2.3-1_amd64.deb
Fedora / RHEL / openSUSEsudo dnf install ./folderblog-0.2.3-1.x86_64.rpm
autonomix-cliautonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/folderblog

The packages and a plain tarball are on the v0.2.3 release. New to folderblog? Start with the guide, or run folderblog guide.

item.title: Hyprfall: a jungle platformer native to Omarchy
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Remember the summer of ’82? One stiff red button, a thousand screens of jungle, and a crocodile that still owes you an apology. Hyprfall is that spirit as a native Omarchy app: swing on ethernet cables, hop the anti-AI garden gnomes, and find 32 treasures before the clock runs out.
item.content:encoded:
Remember the summer of ’82? One stiff red button, a thousand screens of jungle, and a crocodile that still owes you an apology. Hyprfall is that spirit as a native Omarchy app: swing on ethernet cables, hop the anti-AI garden gnomes, and find 32 treasures before the clock runs out.

hyprfall.ninepointlabs.com · v0.1.0 on GitHub

What you are playing

You get twenty minutes, three lives, and 255 screens of jungle arranged in a ring. Each screen comes from one byte walked with a reversible 8-bit LFSR, so walking left brings back exactly the screens you passed. Same jungle every game; learn it like it is 1983.

Between you and the loot: tarballs, a purple pool of node_modules, rolling logs that knock points off, a python that will kill you (should have used Ruby), dumpster fires, and a pit of garden gnomes waving signs like RTFM, STOP VIBING, and NO AI. When they are quiet, their hats are stepping stones. When they yell, get off.

The signature move is the ethernet cable. Jump for the plug, ride it across, and let go with ↓ or Space. Hold the direction you want and the swing flings you that way. Fumble it and enjoy the tar. Underneath, a tunnel lets you skip three screens up top — watch for firewalls and the bug that works on its machine.

Treasure is worth chasing: Golden Keycaps, Rubies, Arch Idols, and Hypr Crystals. Find all 32 before 0:00.

Native to Omarchy, not bolted on

Hyprfall runs on Quickshell — the same engine as the Omarchy shell. No Electron, no browser, no emulator. On Omarchy there is nothing extra to install.

The whole jungle wears your theme: canopy green, swamp blue, tee logo accent, gnome hats and coats. Run omarchy theme set mid-game and it repaints while you play. Skin, hair, and wood stay fixed so the hero (long wavy hair, beard, black tee) stays recognisable on every theme.

It opens as a centered floating 16:10 window on Hyprland; launch again and it focuses the one already open. F11 goes fullscreen. Vim keys work: h/l to run, k/j to climb.

There is an original adventure-rock soundtrack and a dozen sound effects, all generated from scratch by a little synth in the repo. High scores live in ~/.local/state/hyprfall/save.json.

Grab v0.1.0

Packages for Arch/Omarchy, Debian, and Fedora ship on the v0.1.0 release. Each package was installed on its distro and the game run headless (hyprfall --selftest) before the release went out.

autonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/hyprfall

Or install the .pkg.tar.zst, .deb, or .rpm from the release page, then launch Hyprfall from the app launcher or run hyprfall. Away from Omarchy you need a Wayland desktop with Quickshell; without an Omarchy theme it falls back to a built-in Tokyo Night palette.

MIT licensed. An affectionate parody — nothing from any 1982 cartridge, and the protesting gnomes are a joke at a debate, not at anyone in it. Some of them make good points, and they all have excellent signs.

item.title: Linkguard: catch dead links and swap in archived copies
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Every blog rots a little. The post you wrote two years ago still reads fine, but a third of its outbound links now land on a 404, a parked domain, or a redesign that ate the page. Linkguard is a free GitHub Action that finds those links in a Jekyll, Hugo, or folderblog site and points readers to an archived copy instead.
item.content:encoded:
Every blog rots a little. The post you wrote two years ago still reads fine, but a third of its outbound links now land on a 404, a parked domain, or a redesign that ate the page. Linkguard is a free GitHub Action that finds those links in a Jekyll, Hugo, or folderblog site and points readers to an archived copy instead.

linkguard.persistwise.com · v0.1.0 on GitHub

What it does

Drop it into a weekly workflow and Linkguard walks your content, pulls every outbound link out of the markdown and HTML (skipping code blocks, comments, relative links, and private addresses), and checks each one. Every link comes back as one of four results:

  • ok works, or only moved from http to https
  • moved still works but redirects somewhere else, so you may want to update it
  • dead is a 404 or 410, or an outage that survived retries
  • blocked is bot protection (401, 403, 999), and Linkguard never calls those dead

For each link it also asks the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine for a snapshot. When a dead link has a good one, the report hands you the archived URL. Results land in the run’s job summary as a table, as warning annotations on the exact source lines, and as JSON and markdown report files.

It checks politely: one request per host at a time, at most four in flight, retries with backoff, and Retry-After honoured.

Two modes, no account required

Lookup-only is the default. No secrets, nothing captured, just checks and existing snapshots.

Snapshot mode turns on when you add your own free Internet Archive keys as repo secrets. Linkguard then asks Save Page Now to capture working links that have no recent snapshot, so a copy exists before the page dies. Captures count against your own Internet Archive account and are paced to six a minute, so a first run over 100 links can take a while.

Fix it with a pull request

Set open-pr: true and Linkguard opens a pull request that replaces each dead link with its web.archive.org copy, exactly where it appears and nowhere else. The PR lists every swap and says plainly that each one is an archived copy, not the original. It never pushes to your default branch, so you review before anything changes.

Get started

# .github/workflows/linkguard.yml
name: Linkguard
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '17 6 * * 1' # weekly
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  links:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ninepointlabs/linkguard@v0.1.0

It detects your site type from the repo layout, or you can pass site-type and your own paths. Ready-made workflows for Jekyll, Hugo, and folderblog are in the repo’s examples/ folder, and the README documents every input and output.

The free tier checks 100 unique links per run; anything past that is skipped, and the log says how many.

Honest limits and privacy

This is a first release. Snapshot capture and open-pr are covered by mocked tests so far, the Internet Archive doesn’t publish its rate limits, and its availability API sometimes misses a snapshot that exists. A link that’s down for a GitHub runner can still be up for people, so read the report before you merge.

There’s no telemetry and no Linkguard server. Only link URLs go to archive.org; your file contents never leave the runner. MIT licensed. Problems go in the issue tracker.

item.title: Bahá’í Reader 0.1.2: Fedora starts clean, passages cite their source
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Bahá’í Reader already gave you offline English collections, downloadable prayer languages, and a GTK 4 window that follows your Omarchy theme. 0.1.2 is a small release with one hard fix and one reading improvement: the Fedora RPM starts again on a fresh install, and every passage ends with a citation.
item.content:encoded:
Bahá’í Reader already gave you offline English collections, downloadable prayer languages, and a GTK 4 window that follows your Omarchy theme. 0.1.2 is a small release with one hard fix and one reading improvement: the Fedora RPM starts again on a fresh install, and every passage ends with a citation.

Fedora’s cairo typelib

On an up-to-date Fedora 43, the v0.1.1 RPM failed at startup with Typelib file for namespace 'cairo' not found. Fedora’s python3-gobject-base update dropped its dependency on gobject-introspection, and that package is the one that ships cairo-1.0.typelib. Without it, from gi.repository import Gtk never gets off the ground.

The RPM now depends on gobject-introspection directly. If you hit that error on Fedora, upgrade to 0.1.2 and reinstall; Arch and Debian packages were already fine.

Passage citations

Each passage now closes with an italic citation line. Prayers show the author (from the feed’s AuthorId). The Writings show author, book, and section or number — Hidden Words, the Aqdas, Some Answered Questions, Days of Remembrance, Riḍván messages, and the rest. The API does not publish page numbers, so those stay out.

You can quote or save a passage without flipping back to the contents to remember which book you were in.

Grab it

autonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/bahai-reader
# or if you already track it:
autonomix-cli update

Packages (.deb, .rpm, .pkg.tar.zst, AppImage) are on the v0.1.2 release. This is still an independent community app; the texts keep their own attribution in DATA-NOTICE.md.

item.title: Autonomix 0.4: JSON for frontends, and a bar widget that uses it
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Autonomix CLI already tracked your GitHub Releases apps from the terminal, and on Omarchy it could ride along with omarchy update. What it could not do was talk cleanly to another program. Today that changes: 0.4 ships a JSON surface for every command, and omarchy-autonomix is the first bar widget built on top of it.
item.content:encoded:
Autonomix CLI already tracked your GitHub Releases apps from the terminal, and on Omarchy it could ride along with omarchy update. What it could not do was talk cleanly to another program. Today that changes: 0.4 ships a JSON surface for every command, and omarchy-autonomix is the first bar widget built on top of it.

Why it matters

GitHub-release apps live outside the Arch repos. You want a count on the bar, a panel to install or update, and a password dialog — not a second terminal ritual. The CLI stays the source of truth in ~/.autonomix/config.json; the widget is just a frontend that speaks --json.

What’s new in autonomix-cli 0.4

  • --json on every command. add, list, check, update, install, and remove print structured objects on stdout and keep progress on stderr. Errors come back as {"error": "..."} with exit code 1.
  • list, install <app>, and remove <app> for frontends that need to drive one app at a time. remove stops tracking; it does not uninstall.
  • check and update take app names — by name, repo, owner/repo, or URL — so you are not forced to refresh everything.
  • add owner/repo works without pasting a full URL.
  • pkexec when there is no terminal, so a graphical frontend gets Omarchy’s polkit dialog instead of a silent sudo failure.
  • No surprise downgrades. Update detection now compares versions the way pacman does; only a newer release counts. The Omarchy post-update hook will not yank you backward.

Grab 0.4.1, not 0.4.0: the first 0.4 release mistook /dev/null for a terminal and reached for sudo from the bar. 0.4.1 asks the terminal driver properly, so installs from the widget get a password prompt.

The new Omarchy bar widget

omarchy-autonomix is a Quickshell plugin: a package icon with an update count, and a panel that lists tracked apps, installs or updates them, and lets you track owner/repo or a GitHub URL without opening a terminal. Middle-click the icon to check GitHub now. It needs autonomix-cli 0.4+ at /usr/bin or /usr/local/bin.

git clone https://github.com/ninepointlabs/omarchy-autonomix ~/Projects/omarchy-autonomix
~/Projects/omarchy-autonomix/install.sh
omarchy plugin enable ninepointlabs.autonomix

Grab the CLI

autonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/autonomix-cli
# or update if you already track it:
autonomix-cli update

Packages for Arch, Debian/Ubuntu, and Fedora are on the v0.4.1 release. If you are still on the October 11 updater post, this is the next chapter: same list of apps, now reachable from the bar.

item.title: fm-cli 0.3.5: Pick your From, and calendar that finds you
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: fm-cli already lived in the terminal. Two small releases today, 0.3.4 and 0.3.5, fix the kind of sharp edges you only notice once you use a tool every day — and both came in with help from outside the house.
item.content:encoded:
fm-cli already lived in the terminal. Two small releases today, 0.3.4 and 0.3.5, fix the kind of sharp edges you only notice once you use a tool every day — and both came in with help from outside the house.

Send as the address you mean

Fastmail’s web UI has a default identity, but Identity/get does not reorder itself around that choice. fm-cli always composed from identities[0]. That is fine if you have one address. It is wrong the moment you have a few.

You can now set the default yourself:

fm-cli settings from me@example.com
# or for a one-off / script:
export FM_DEFAULT_FROM=me@example.com

The address is matched case-insensitively against your identities. The environment wins over the stored setting; unset or unmatched falls back to the first identity. New composes in the TUI, drafts and sends with an empty From, and offline sends replayed by fm-cli sync all respect it. Tab still cycles the list in the order Fastmail returned.

Ask the server who you are on CalDAV

Calendar and contacts setup guessed the principal path as /dav/principals/user/<login email>/. Cyrus folds dots in the local part to underscores (noah.hopping → noah_hopping), so those accounts got 404 “Mailbox does not exist” and never discovered a calendar home.

0.3.5 roots both CalDAV and CardDAV clients at the DAV context URL and reads current-user-principal with a PROPFIND (RFC 6764 bootstrapping). The href the server returns drives home-set discovery. The PROPFIND is issued directly so the trailing slash on /dav/ survives — go-webdav’s helper collapses it and Cyrus answers 405.

If your login has a dot and calendar never came up, upgrade and try fm-cli auth dav again.

Thanks

Both fixes started with reports and patches from Noah Hopping (@fsnoah). The From-identity work landed in #3; the principal discovery in #4. That is the kind of contribution that turns a personal tool into something other people can trust.

Grab it

# Omarchy
omarchy-mise-install github:ninepointlabs/fm-cli fm-cli

# mise
mise use -g github:ninepointlabs/fm-cli@latest

# autonomix-cli
autonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/fm-cli

Or take a .pkg.tar.zst, .deb, .rpm, or tarball from the v0.3.5 release.

item.title: Rune 0.8: From ODF experiment to a word processor you can install
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Yesterday’s Rune post was about a principle: ODF is home, DOCX is a guest. Since then Rune has gone from 0.2 to 0.8.4 in about two days, and it has stopped being an idea about formats and started being an app you can install and write a book in.
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday’s Rune post was about a principle: ODF is home, DOCX is a guest. Since then Rune has gone from 0.2 to 0.8.4 in about two days, and it has stopped being an idea about formats and started being an app you can install and write a book in.

Install it like a real app

Every GitHub release now ships packages for Arch/Omarchy, Debian 13 and Fedora 42, with a desktop entry. The easiest path keeps it updated for you:

autonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/rune

The everyday editor filled in

  • A File menu with save-button states and autosave.
  • Font and text-color pickers, and a toolbar that fits any window: Table and alignment menus, with a ⋯ overflow for the rest.
  • A Table menu: insert rows and columns, delete a table.
  • A command palette on Ctrl+K.
  • Pages and margins: a real page view, Page setup, and paper size picked from your locale.
  • Headers and footers edited in place, with page number and page count fields that round-trip through both ODF and .docx.

Rune writes its own ODF now

Rune used to lean on Qt’s document writer, and it kept losing things: headings saved as bold text, nested tables lost content, a table after a list could vanish. Rune now writes the whole .odt itself: real Heading 1–6 styles, links, lists that keep their numbering across interruptions, and tables with widths, borders, merged cells and nesting. If ODF is the home format, Rune has to be a good citizen of it, and now it is one.

Tools for people writing long things

0.8.3 added author tooling:

  • Headings from the toolbar (Ctrl+Alt+0–3) and an outline sidebar with chapters, scenes and word counts. Drag a section to move it in one undo step.
  • Story notes saved inside the file.
  • Sources from a form, CSL-JSON or BibTeX, with citations (Ctrl+Shift+C) in APA 7, MLA 9, Chicago author-date or IEEE, and a bibliography that keeps up with every edit.

Citations survive a trip through .docx. Word and LibreOffice see the text, and Rune finds the citations again when the file comes back.

AI edits that don’t wreck your paragraphs

The AI can read your notes and sources, cite with [@key], and add sources, which are marked unreviewed until you check them. 0.8.4 fixed a nasty one: models copied 80-column line wraps into their edits, and every wrap became a paragraph break. The context now goes out one paragraph per line, and slightly garbled quotes still match. The same edit came out clean in 15 of 15 live ChatGPT runs, where every run checked before had broken paragraphs.

See it first

The site now has screenshots, a narrated 1:47 demo recorded from the real app, and a seven-page how-to guide covering formatting, pages, the AI, writing a book, and citations. Under all of it are 487 automated checks.

ODF by default still holds. The difference now is that Rune gives you a real reason to choose it.

item.title: Speakeasy 0.3: Your bots can start the tasks now
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Speakeasy already kept coding agents in named, hidden terminals so you could see what was running without drowning in windows. As of 0.3, other programs can hand it work the same way you do from the bar.
item.content:encoded:
Speakeasy already kept coding agents in named, hidden terminals so you could see what was running without drowning in windows. As of 0.3, other programs can hand it work the same way you do from the bar.

An MCP server on stdio

speakeasy mcp speaks the Model Context Protocol over standard input and output. No network port, no daemon to babysit. Point Claude Code, Grok Bot, Hermes, or any other MCP client at the binary and it gets four tools:

  • list_agents — which agents are installed and visible, with models and effort levels
  • find_repo — where a GitHub repo is checked out on this machine
  • create_task — start a task with title, description, agent, and optional model, effort, and repo or folder
  • list_tasks — what is already running, so a bot does not start a duplicate

A bot watching your repos can pick Claude or Codex, write the brief, and park the job in the right local checkout. It shows up in your Speakeasy list like anything you started yourself. The client’s name is stored as the task’s origin, and Speakeasy leaves your new-task picker defaults alone.

Approvals stay yours

The MCP path deliberately cannot pass extra agent arguments, so a bot cannot flip permission prompts off. It also cannot peek at a task’s screen, type into it, or stop it. The agent still asks you before risky actions; you still answer.

find_repo strips credentials out of remote URLs before it reports them. Add the MCP server only to clients you trust, same as you would any tool that can start processes in your project folders.

Titles and prompts off the process list

0.3.1 closes a quieter hole. The Omarchy panel used to put the task title and description on the speakeasy new command line, where any other user on the machine could read them with ps. They now go over stdin as one line of JSON (--stdin-json). The CLI already avoided stuffing prompts into argv for normal use; the panel catches up.

Try it

speakeasy mcp
# or wire it into Claude Code:
claude mcp add speakeasy -- ~/.local/bin/speakeasy mcp

Upgrade with your usual Omarchy plugin path, or pull ninepointlabs/speakeasy and run ./install.sh. If your workflow is “bot finds the problem, I approve the fix,” Speakeasy is now the handoff.

item.title: Kestrel: Post to X from Your Terminal (or Let Your AI Do It)
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: If you have ever wanted to fire off a tweet without leaving your terminal, or better yet, hand the keys to an AI agent and trust it not to burn through your X API budget, Kestrel has you covered.
item.content:encoded:
If you have ever wanted to fire off a tweet without leaving your terminal, or better yet, hand the keys to an AI agent and trust it not to burn through your X API budget, Kestrel has you covered.

Kestrel is a Rust CLI that posts to X (Twitter) and doubles as an MCP server so AI agents can post through it. The killer feature: a hard daily post limit, shared between the CLI and the MCP server. Your agent might be chatty, but Kestrel knows when to say “that’s enough for today.”

Two modes, one binary

From the terminal, it is dead simple:

kestrel post "Hello world"
kestrel post "check this out" --image ./photo.png
kestrel status         # Posts today: 3/50 (6%)

Fire up the MCP server with kestrel serve and suddenly Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or Hermes can post on your behalf with exactly the same guardrails. No separate config, no backdoor. If the daily limit is hit, the MCP tool returns an error result instead of posting. Your credit card stays safe.

The economics of X posting in 2026

Here is the part that makes Kestrel genuinely useful instead of just fun. Since February 2026, X’s API is pay-per-use with no free tier. Every post costs real money:

  • Plain text tweet: $0.015
  • Tweet with a URL: $0.200 (yes, 13x more)
  • Summoned reply: $0.010

A link surcharge that steep means one careless agent posting URLs could run up a bill fast. Kestrel’s daily limit is your safety net. At 50 posts per day, plain text costs $22.50/month. With links mixed in at 30%, that jumps to $90/month. Kestrel makes sure you know exactly where you stand.

Built to be boring (in the best way)

The config lives in ~/.config/kestrel/config.toml with 0600 permissions. State is tracked in a tiny JSON file that resets at midnight local time. One binary, one config file, one state file. No daemon, no database, no cloud service. It works the same whether you type kestrel post or your AI agent does.

The MCP server exposes exactly two tools: kestrel_post and kestrel_status. That is it. No read access, no timeline scraping, no DMs. Kestrel is built for one job and it does not overreach.

Worth a look if

You post from the terminal, you run AI agents that need controlled X access, or you just appreciate a well-scoped Rust tool that respects your wallet. The repo has a clear README with pricing tables, troubleshooting guides for every HTTP error code, and a one-command install via cargo install --path ..

item.title: Why Rune Treats DOCX as a Guest, Not a Host
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: I’ve been building Rune, our word processor, and I just made a decision that I expect a few people to push back on: DOCX is not a first-class citizen. ODF is the native format. DOCX is import and export only.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve been building Rune, our word processor, and I just made a decision that I expect a few people to push back on: DOCX is not a first-class citizen. ODF is the native format. DOCX is import and export only.

Here’s the thing I had to talk myself out of first.

My first instinct was to make DOCX a first-class format alongside ODF, because it’s convenient. DOCX is what the business world runs on, it’s what shows up in every email attachment, and treating it as a second-tier citizen felt like making life harder for anyone who has to interoperate with the rest of the planet. That instinct was really just me optimizing for my own convenience, not for what Rune should actually be.

Then I looked honestly at how often I actually create documents that need to be DOCX. Rarely. Almost never, really. Most of what I write doesn’t care what the underlying format is, it cares about being readable, editable, and not locked to one vendor’s whims. The cases where DOCX truly matters are the cases where I’m handing something to someone else’s pipeline, and for that, export now and again is plenty.

So that settled it for me: if ODF is ever going to get real traction, and if we actually want to see the world move away from a single-vendor format as the default assumption, somebody has to stop treating DOCX as equal. Every tool that makes DOCX the comfortable default, even a little, is one more vote for the status quo. Rune is my vote the other way. ODF is home. DOCX is a well-supported guest, not a roommate.

The “well-supported” part matters, because I’m not interested in making DOCX support bad out of principle. Nobody wins if opening a .docx in Rune mangles someone’s formatting. So on the backend, DOCX import and export runs through the LibreOffice engine. LibreOffice has put in literally decades of work getting that conversion right, through every quirky OOXML edge case Microsoft has shipped over the years. There’s no reason for me to reinvent that wheel badly when I can lean on work that’s already excellent. Rune gets to stay focused on being a genuinely good ODF-native editor, and the DOCX bridge gets to be solid because someone else already paid the tuition for that problem.

That’s the shape of it: ODF by default, DOCX by door, LibreOffice doing the heavy lifting at the threshold. If you want to see where Rune is headed, rune.ninepointlabs.com has more.

item.title: Autonomix Now Plugs Straight Into the Omarchy Updater
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Remember Autonomix CLI, the terminal tool that tracks your GitHub Releases apps? It had one nagging flaw: it wouldn’t update anything unless you remembered to open it and ask. Which, if you’re like most people, is never.
item.content:encoded:
Remember Autonomix CLI, the terminal tool that tracks your GitHub Releases apps? It had one nagging flaw: it wouldn’t update anything unless you remembered to open it and ask. Which, if you’re like most people, is never.

That’s fixed now. Autonomix just picked up a real check and update command, and on Omarchy it hooks straight into the system updater, so your GitHub-sourced apps get refreshed in the same breath as everything else.

What’s new

  • autonomix-cli check lists every tracked app with an update available, no TUI required.
  • autonomix-cli update [-y] installs those updates non-interactively, the -y flag skips the confirmation prompt entirely.
  • It only touches apps installed through your actual package manager (dpkg, rpm, pacman). Anything living as a loose binary on PATH, or managed through Flatpak/Snap, gets reported and left alone, because blindly overwriting those is how you break things.
  • --version and --help now behave like every other CLI instead of falling through to the TUI.
  • Set GITHUB_TOKEN (or GH_TOKEN) if you’re tracking enough repos to hit GitHub’s 60-requests-an-hour API limit; it bumps you to 5,000.

The Omarchy part

This is the fun bit. Drop the included hook into Omarchy’s update pipeline and Autonomix updates ride along for free every time you run omarchy update:

install -m755 contrib/omarchy/autonomix.hook ~/.config/omarchy/hooks/post-update.d/autonomix.hook

That’s it. One omarchy update now refreshes your system packages and whatever you’re tracking through Autonomix, no separate step to remember.

Autonomix CLI on GitHub →

Grab the latest release, or if you’re already on it, go build and you’re there. If you haven’t tried Autonomix at all yet, the first post has the full rundown.

item.title: Jubako: Microsoft Access, Without the Hard Parts
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: You know that moment when you open a folder and find budget_FINAL_v3.xlsx, budget_FINAL_v3 (1).csv, and budget REAL FINAL.xlsx all staring back at you? Spreadsheets are great until they aren’t – until you need to ask “which customers haven’t paid yet” and you’re doing mental gymnastics with filters and color-coded cells.
item.content:encoded:
You know that moment when you open a folder and find budget_FINAL_v3.xlsx, budget_FINAL_v3 (1).csv, and budget REAL FINAL.xlsx all staring back at you? Spreadsheets are great until they aren’t – until you need to ask “which customers haven’t paid yet” and you’re doing mental gymnastics with filters and color-coded cells.

Jubako on GitHub | jubako.ninepointlabs.com

Jubako (pronounced joo-bah-koh, named after the stacked Japanese lunch boxes) is a simple desktop database for Omarchy Linux. One file, several tables, no SQL required. Think of it as the spirit of old-school Microsoft Access, reimagined for people who would rather get things done than learn a query language.

Drop a Spreadsheet, Get a Database

The killer feature is the import. Drag a CSV or Excel file onto the window and Jubako figures out what each column is – words, whole numbers, decimals, dates, yes/no values. It shows you its best guesses before writing anything, so you can correct a column that got tagged as “words” when it’s really a date column. A multi-sheet workbook becomes one table per sheet. No ceremony, no setup.

Once your data is in, you can browse it as a grid, type row-by-row in a form, filter with rules like “Status is not Delivered AND Total over 100,” and save those filters as named views. Need to print? The report designer gives you a live preview, groups rows with subtotals, and exports to PDF. Your spreadsheet just grew up.

Your AI Agent Can Drive It Too

Jubako ships with an MCP server, which means Claude Code (or any MCP-capable agent) can do everything the app can do. “Take this spreadsheet and make me a database” works as a natural-language command. The tools cover the full surface: create databases, import spreadsheets, list and filter rows, add and update records, design reports, export to CSV or Excel or PDF. Twenty-seven tools in total, all over stdio.

Safety is taken seriously: file paths are checked against approved folders, spreadsheet formulas are never executed, server passwords are never saved, and destructive operations ask first.

Under the Hood

Jubako is a Qt Quick desktop app with a Python core. By default your database is a single SQLite file (.jubadb) in your Documents folder – copy it, back it up, email it. If you already run PostgreSQL or MySQL, you can point Jubako at that instead. The app follows your Omarchy theme, light or dark, and changes with it when you switch.

Installation is one command on Arch/Omarchy, Debian, or Fedora – packages are on the releases page. Or clone the repo and run from source. It’s MIT-licensed and actively developed, with a growing test suite that covers type guessing, path safety, CSV and Excel import/export, reports, and the MCP server.

If your spreadsheets have been quietly running your life, Jubako is a clean upgrade. Same data, less chaos, and a lunch box metaphor you didn’t know you needed.

Jubako on GitHub

item.title: Idea: a CLI for the “wait, I had something” moments
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: You know the feeling. You’re three levels deep in a terminal, wiring up some pipeline, and an idea pops into your head: “I should really automate that database migration.” Or maybe “What if the cron job just emailed the digest instead?” By the time you finish what you’re doing, the thought is gone, replaced by whatever error message you’re now staring at.
item.content:encoded:
You know the feeling. You’re three levels deep in a terminal, wiring up some pipeline, and an idea pops into your head: “I should really automate that database migration.” Or maybe “What if the cron job just emailed the digest instead?” By the time you finish what you’re doing, the thought is gone, replaced by whatever error message you’re now staring at.

Ideas on GitHub is the smallest possible answer to that problem. It’s a single Go binary that appends numbered ideas to a markdown file. No database, no daemon, no web UI. Just idea "your thought here" and you’re back to work.

How it works

idea "Add retry logic to the API client"
idea "Switch the blog to folderblog instead of Hugo"
idea "Write a cron job that posts a daily project highlight"

Each one gets the next number. When you want to see them:

idea -l

And when you’ve actually done the thing, or decided it was a terrible idea after all:

idea -r 2         # remove idea 2
idea -r 1-3       # remove ideas 1 through 3
idea -r 1,5,9     # remove specific ones

After removal, the remaining ideas renumber themselves from 1. It’s all atomic, too: if any number in your range is invalid, nothing gets removed. No half-done cleanups.

Why it’s great

It’s written in Go with zero dependencies beyond the standard library. The binary is small, the build is instant, and the storage format is just a markdown file under a # Ideas heading in ~/Documents/Ideas/ideas.md. You can point it anywhere with IDEAS_FILE if you want per-project idea files. There’s nothing to break, nothing to upgrade, and nothing to regret installing.

Sometimes the best tool is the one that does exactly one thing and then gets out of your way. Ideas doesn’t try to be Notion. It doesn’t try to organize, categorize, prioritize, or remind. It just writes down the thing you thought of so you can get back to the thing you were doing.

Install

git clone https://github.com/ninepointlabs/ideas.git
cd ideas
make build
sudo make install

That’s it. idea lands in /usr/local/bin and you’re ready to stop losing thoughts to the void.

Grab it at github.com/ninepointlabs/ideas and give your stray thoughts a home.

item.title: folderblog: Save a File, Publish a Blog
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Here’s a radical idea: what if publishing a blog post was exactly as hard as hitting Ctrl+S? No build step. No git push. No front matter to remember. No deploy command. Just a Markdown file in a folder, and a few seconds later, it’s live.
item.content:encoded:
Here’s a radical idea: what if publishing a blog post was exactly as hard as hitting Ctrl+S? No build step. No git push. No front matter to remember. No deploy command. Just a Markdown file in a folder, and a few seconds later, it’s live.

That’s folderblog. And it actually delivers.

folderblog on GitHub →  |  Website & video tour →

A folder is a blog

folderblog is a single Rust binary that runs quietly in the background, watching ~/Blogs. Every subfolder is its own independent blog — its own theme, its own settings, its own publish target. You write in any editor, save the file, and the background service notices, waits for the burst of saves to settle, builds the site in a fresh folder, and pushes it live. If anything breaks, the live site stays exactly as it was — folderblog never half-updates it, and you get a desktop notification telling you what went wrong.

GitHub Pages works with zero ongoing clicks. Log in once, and folderblog new myblog creates the repository, turns on Pages, and publishes your first post. Custom domains too — it even prints the DNS records you need. Not a GitHub person? It also publishes to any git branch, or runs any command you give it: rsync, rclone, wrangler, Netlify CLI, whatever.

Themes with no ceiling

folderblog’s engine handles content, feeds, and sitemaps. Everything else — every byte of HTML, every stylesheet, every JSON search index — belongs to the theme. Themes are Jinja templates that can produce any layout and any file format. One template can render tag pages, year archives, paginated series. A theme can even generate its own search index.

To prove the engine doesn’t interfere, we gave three coding agents the same blog, its AGENTS.md contract, and a one-line design brief. None of them needed a change to the engine. The screenshots in this post? Same blog, four different themes, all agent-built.

The little things that make it good

Posts don’t need front matter. The title comes from your first heading, the address from the filename, the date from when folderblog first saw it, recorded once, so editing or syncing never moves it. Delete a file, and the post is unpublished. There’s a built-in photo gallery: folderblog gallery on, drop pictures into a folder, and only resized copies ever reach the site (your originals with GPS metadata stay local). Drafts only appear in preview. folderblog check catches template errors, broken links, and feed problems before anything goes live.

It runs on Linux — packages for Arch, Debian/Ubuntu, and Fedora, plus a static binary. Written in Rust, MIT licensed, git is the only dependency.

folderblog is the kind of tool that makes you wonder why blogs were ever harder than this. If you’ve been putting off starting one because the tooling felt like a chore — this might be your excuse. Grab it from the repo, follow the step-by-step guide, and save a file.

item.title: Even the fork gets a fork
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: The Omarchy ecosystem sprouted a few new branches this week. Quiet growth, the kind you notice only when you step back and count.
item.content:encoded:
The Omarchy ecosystem sprouted a few new branches this week. Quiet growth, the kind you notice only when you step back and count.

fsnoah forked fm-cli, the Fastmail client I built in Go. That is the best kind of compliment. Someone looked at a terminal email client and thought “I want to improve that.” They even opened an issue asking for configurable default sending identities, which tells me they are actually using it and want it to work better for them. That is not a drive-by star. That is engagement.

Three new repos landed: quill, kestrel, and a machine setup toolkit for Omarchy. Quill joined Omostrich’s website navigation right away, so whatever it is, it earned a landing-page spot before most people even noticed it existed. The canon repo got three commits in one night — daily sync, a shared memory directive, and the kind of infrastructure polish that nobody tweets about but keeps the agents from drifting apart.

The agents themselves kept up their quiet coordination. Ted sent his Facebook digests. Cromm ran selftests. Neither one needed me. That is the whole point of having agents: they do their jobs and only tap you on the shoulder when something actually breaks.

On the plugin side, the usual suspects kept getting published. My-Azeroth-Life hit five gh-pages publishes this week alone. The tech blog hit three. That is a lot of content from systems that write themselves. I built a publishing pipeline that runs with almost no human intervention, and it is starting to feel normal. That is probably the most impressive thing about this week: none of this feels impressive anymore. It just works.

item.title: fm-cli: Fastmail, Minus the Browser Tab
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: You know the feeling: you’re deep in the terminal, in the zone, and then you need to check your email. You switch to the browser, wait for Fastmail to load, wade through some newsletters, and five minutes later you’ve forgotten why you opened it in the first place.
item.content:encoded:
You know the feeling: you’re deep in the terminal, in the zone, and then you need to check your email. You switch to the browser, wait for Fastmail to load, wade through some newsletters, and five minutes later you’ve forgotten why you opened it in the first place.

fm-cli fixes that. It’s a full Fastmail client that lives in your terminal, built in Go, all keystrokes, no browser tab needed.

fm-cli on GitHub →

Mail, calendar, contacts — all from the keyboard

fm-cli talks directly to Fastmail’s JMAP API. No IMAP workarounds, no polling, no stored copies of your mail on someone else’s server. It’s the real thing, and it’s also the engine behind the Fastmail plugin for Omarchy, so it’s battle-tested every day.

The TUI gives you everything you’d expect: folders, threaded conversations, clickable links, reply-all, forward, flag, archive, move, delete. Compose in $EDITOR with contact autocomplete that actually works. A two-week calendar agenda and a contacts browser. Inline images, if your terminal supports it. And an offline mode that caches mail in SQLite so you can read and draft on a plane — changes sync back when you reconnect.

Scripting that doesn’t fight you

Here’s where fm-cli really shines. Every command accepts --json and prints exactly one JSON object — {"ok": true, "data": …} on success, {"ok": false, "error": "…", "code": "auth|usage|network|remote|busy"} on failure. That means you can pipe it into jq, drive it from shell scripts, or build automation around your mailbox without parsing human-readable output or worrying about edge cases:

fm-cli box view inbox --limit 20 --json | jq '.data[].subject'

The watch command holds a live push connection open and prints a JSON line for every change — new mail, read status, folder moves. One connection per account, no polling, no rate limits.

Auth you don’t have to think about

Sign in with fm-cli auth login and it opens Fastmail’s consent page in your browser. Approve it there, and the tokens go straight into your system keyring. They refresh themselves. You never copy a token. If you’re on a headless machine, FM_API_TOKEN, FM_EMAIL, and FM_APP_PASSWORD in the environment stand in for the keyring.

Calendar and contacts use CalDAV and CardDAV with a Fastmail app password — fm-cli auth dav stores it, and you’re done.

Install it

On Omarchy: omarchy-mise-install github:ninepointlabs/fm-cli fm-cli

Everywhere else: mise use -g github:ninepointlabs/fm-cli@latest

Releases also ship .pkg.tar.zst, .deb, .rpm, and plain tarballs for Linux and macOS. Go 1.26 or newer, no C toolchain needed. Clone it, go build, and you’re off.

If your email lives on Fastmail and you spend a lot of time in the terminal, fm-cli is one of those tools that makes you wonder how you managed without it. Grab it from the repo and reclaim that browser tab.

item.title: Bahá’í Reader: A Quiet GTK 4 Reader That Follows Your Desktop Theme
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Here’s a thing you don’t see every day: a Linux desktop app built for quiet, focused reading of Bahá’í sacred texts, and it tracks your Omarchy desktop theme live, every single second.
item.content:encoded:
Here’s a thing you don’t see every day: a Linux desktop app built for quiet, focused reading of Bahá’í sacred texts, and it tracks your Omarchy desktop theme live, every single second.

Bahá’í Reader is a standalone GTK 4 app. No shell plugin required. No Omarchy dependency — it just reads your desktop’s colors.toml and follows along. Light mode in the morning, dark mode at night, sepia when you’re feeling fancy. The app window is deliberately plain and undecorated, letting your window manager (Hyprland, presumably) supply the borders.

What’s inside

English ships with all ten collections available from BahaiPrayers.net — 2,616 records covering Prayers, Hidden Words (Arabic and Persian divisions), Gleanings, the Kitáb-i-Íqán, Tablets of Bahá’u’lláh, and more. That includes 190 Aqdas paragraphs, 107 Questions and Answers, 84 chapters of Some Answered Questions — it’s comprehensive.

Beyond English, the app catalogs 112 prayer languages. Pick one, download its collections, and you’re reading offline. Everything’s stored as permanent user data, not cache. A failed download leaves existing content untouched.

The feature list that matters

  • Full-text search across any section, completely offline
  • Topic filtering and saved passages
  • Last-passage restoration (pick up where you left off)
  • Collapsible table of contents that follows the API’s category structure
  • Previous/Next navigation that stays within the current category or book
  • Independent reading font and sizing, separate from the interface

One detail I appreciate: Ctrl+F searches, Ctrl+D saves, Ctrl+Q quits, Escape restores navigation. The keyboard shortcuts are sensible and discoverable.

Why it’s neat

Most religious-text apps are either a website wrapper or a bloated Electron thing. Bahá’í Reader is neither — it’s a native GTK 4 window, a Python script (reader.py), and local data files. The whole install is a single .deb, .rpm, or .pkg.tar.zst package. There’s even an AppImage if you’re into that.

It builds and releases with GitHub Actions, testing on Debian 12, Fedora 43, and Arch containers before tagged releases ever see daylight. The code is MIT licensed, the texts have their own attribution in DATA-NOTICE.md, and everything’s cleanly separated.

If you run Omarchy and want a reader that blends into your desktop instead of fighting it, give it a look. Grab the latest release and see if it fits.

Bahá’í Reader is part of the Nine Point Labs family of open-source projects, built for the Omarchy Linux desktop ecosystem.
